vignette: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department due to sudden-onset severe dyspnea, orthopnea, and cold diaphoresis. Five days ago, he experienced 3 hours of substernal chest pressure that resolved spontaneously, for which he did not seek medical care. Blood pressure is 86/52 mm Hg, pulse is 118/min and regular, and respirations are 32/min with an oxygen saturation of 88% on ambient air. Physical examination reveals cool, clammy extremities, jugular venous distension, and bilateral diffuse crackles throughout both lung fields. Cardiac auscultation demonstrates a soft S1, a prominent S3 gallop, and a new harsh, blowing early systolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex that radiates to the left axilla. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates posteromedial papillary muscle rupture and severe mitral regurgitation. Pulmonary artery catheterization shows a mean pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 32 mm Hg with prominent systolic peaks (giant v waves).
question: Which of the following combinations of left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV), left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV), and forward stroke volume is most expected in this patient compared to baseline?

options.A: Increased LVEDV, Decreased LVESV, Decreased forward stroke volume
options.B: Increased LVEDV, Increased LVESV, Decreased forward stroke volume
options.C: Decreased LVEDV, Decreased LVESV, Increased forward stroke volume
options.D: Normal LVEDV, Increased LVESV, Normal forward stroke volume

high_yield_pearl: Acute mitral regurgitation (e.g., post-MI papillary muscle rupture) features increased preload (increased LVEDV) and decreased afterload due to retrograde ejection into the low-impedance left atrium. This low-resistance outflow allows near-complete LV emptying during systole, resulting in decreased LVESV and increased total stroke volume; however, because a large regurgitant fraction flows backward into the noncompliant left atrium, forward stroke volume (systemic cardiac output) drops precipitously, inducing pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock.
tactics_and_technique:
Step 1: Diagnose the underlying lesion. Acute respiratory distress and cardiogenic shock 3 to 7 days after an untreated myocardial infarction with a new apical systolic murmur and giant 'v' waves on pulmonary artery catheterization points directly to acute severe mitral regurgitation secondary to posteromedial papillary muscle rupture (posterior descending artery territory).
Step 2: Trace diastolic filling (Preload/LVEDV). During diastole, the left ventricle receives normal pulmonary venous return plus the large volume of regurgitated blood stored in the unconditioned, stiff left atrium under high pressure. This marked volume overload leads to an increased LVEDV.
Step 3: Analyze systolic ejection and afterload (LVESV). In systole, the left ventricle ejects simultaneously into two parallel conduits: anterograde into the high-resistance aorta and retrograde into the low-pressure/low-impedance left atrium. Because effective ventricular afterload is drastically diminished, the LV empties vigorously and more completely, resulting in a decreased LVESV and elevated ejection fraction.
Step 4: Differentiate total versus forward stroke volume. Although total stroke volume (regurgitant volume + forward volume) is increased, forward stroke volume (net systemic delivery) is markedly decreased, leading to systemic hypotension. Eliminate distractors that model chronic decompensated systolic failure (where LVESV is increased) or cardiac tamponade (where LVEDV is decreased due to external compression).
